analysis.one_liner: Imposes an excise tax on opioid makers and tightens licensing, marketing, and prescribing rules for opioid painkillers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors, sent to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have attacked the prescription opioid crisis at several points at once. It would charge opioid manufacturers an excise tax of one cent per milligram of active opioid they produce, with half the money going to a national drug take-back program and half to substance abuse treatment. It would require federal licenses and ethics training for drug sales representatives who promote Schedule II opioids, automatically suspend FDA approval of ultra-high-dose opioids, require doctors to complete pain-management training before their federal registration to prescribe, and strengthen state prescription monitoring databases. It also ordered studies on Medicare coverage of non-opioid pain treatments and on hospital follow-up after overdoses.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and communities affected by the opioid epidemic: the bill aimed to reduce over-prescribing, curb aggressive marketing of high-dose opioids, fund safe disposal of leftover drugs, and route tax revenue into prevention and treatment programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: The bill would impose a 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on manufacturers of opioid painkillers, with half the revenue funding a national take-back program for safe drug disposal (at least one disposal site per 25,000 residents) and half funding substance abuse prevention and treatment block grants [S3].

Beginning January 1, 2020, drug sales representatives who promote Schedule II opioids (other than methadone) would need a federal license requiring $3,000 registration, training on ethics and CDC prescribing guidelines, a pledge not to engage in deceptive marketing, and annual reports naming the providers they visit and the gifts and samples they give [S3].

The bill would deem any ultra-high-dose opioid — one whose labeled daily dosage exceeds the CDC guideline levels — an imminent hazard to public health, requiring the HHS Secretary to suspend its approval [S3].

Doctors renewing their federal registration to prescribe controlled substances would have to certify they completed training on pain management, addiction risks, and non-opioid alternatives, or limit themselves to 72-hour supplies, and register with their state prescription drug monitoring program [S3].

States receiving federal opioid funding would have to require prescribers to check monitoring databases before prescribing, report prescribing data to federal health and drug enforcement officials, and share data across state borders [S3].
The bill would require a National Academy of Medicine study on whether Medicare covering alternative pain treatments like acupuncture and exercise therapy could reduce opioid prescribing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, opioid manufacturers would bear the excise tax and new reporting duties; doctors would face training and monitoring requirements; and some of the cost could be passed to patients through drug prices.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax on manufacturers would likely be passed through to prices, raising costs for patients who legitimately need opioid pain treatment, and the bill's own GAO study mandate acknowledges the need to keep ensuring that patients who need opioids can access them safely [S3].
Mandatory prescriber training, database checks, and reporting would add administrative burdens for physicians, pharmacists, and state agencies [S3].

The bill would give state law enforcement agencies direct access to prescription drug monitoring databases, which raises privacy concerns for patients whose prescription records would become available to police [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a public health crisis that had killed tens of thousands of Americans a year, and its main costs fell on the pharmaceutical companies that manufactured and marketed the opioids — a deliberate design choice. The real tradeoffs are patient access: the same tools meant to stop over-prescribing (taxes, dose caps, prescribing limits) can make pain treatment harder for people who genuinely need it, and the bill's own study provisions conceded that tension. On balance it was a prevention-and-funding bill paid for by the industry, with privacy and access risks that are real but secondary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2018, and it sat there — with no hearing, no markup, and no vote — until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, killing it.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 23, 2018; no other senator cosponsored it [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the committee took no further action on it [S5].
The bill never advanced past committee and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died, so they never faced the excise tax, forced withdrawal of ultra-high-dose products, or licensed-marketing requirements. Patients awaiting better opioid safeguards and funded treatment programs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who faced no tax or new rules

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on April 23, 2018.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Opioid pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry the bill would tax and regulate
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted them with an excise tax, licensure requirements for their sales forces, and forced withdrawal of ultra-high-dose products; no manufacturer publicly backed it.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party agenda-setters in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor time; with no cosponsors and no committee action, it received no pathway to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never attracted enough support to reveal a clear partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on their production quotas, suspended approval of ultra-high-dose products, and required extra reporting on payments to doctors [S3]. Because the tax and marketing rules were designed to shrink a practice that profits them while harming the public, the industry's interest ran against ordinary people's on this bill.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical sales and marketing (opioid sales reps)
industries.note: Reps promoting Schedule II opioids would have needed a federal license, ethics training, and annual disclosure of provider visits, gifts, and samples [S3].

Prescribers would face mandatory training, monitoring-database registration, and reporting duties, but would also gain clearer guidelines and liability protections around responsible prescribing; patients with chronic pain could face harder access to legitimate prescriptions [S3].
Half the excise tax revenue would flow to SAMHSA's substance abuse treatment block grants and related programs, expanding funded treatment capacity [S3].
